analysis.one_liner: Makes the FRA's railroad safety rulemaking committee—where railroads and labor negotiate safety rules—a permanent part of the law.
analysis.headline: The Railroad Safety and Accountability Act, introduced by one House member with zero cosponsors, sits in a House subcommittee with no action since February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The Railroad Safety Advisory Committee already exists: it is a panel run by the Federal Railroad Administration where freight railroads, Amtrak, passenger advocates, labor unions, and suppliers work out rail safety rules by consensus before the agency adopts them. This bill writes that committee into federal law so it cannot be disbanded or skipped, requires the agency's administrator to meet with it quarterly, and orders an annual report to Congress. It does not itself set any new safety standard—it locks in the process by which railroad safety standards get negotiated.
analysis.who_benefits: The freight railroads, labor unions, and suppliers that hold seats on the committee gain a legally guaranteed, permanent seat at the table for writing the safety rules that govern the industry, and the FRA administrator must formally engage them quarterly. Rail workers and unions gain guaranteed representation for each craft. Communities along rail lines could benefit if the process produces better safety rules, but the bill sets none of its own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Railroads, rail labor unions, and suppliers

how_it_helps.text: Codifies the Railroad Safety Advisory Committee as a permanent statutory body that the FRA administrator must maintain, rather than a committee the agency could restructure or disband.
Requires the FRA administrator to meet quarterly with the committee to consult on regulatory programs, advise it on emerging issues, and receive its recommendations in setting regulatory priorities.

Guarantees at least one seat for each major stakeholder group, including each class of rail labor (operating crews, maintenance of way, shop and mechanical, clerks, dispatchers) plus passenger organizations and local governments.
Requires the committee to report its activities to Congress annually, and exempts it from the federal law that automatically terminates advisory committees.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the committee's operations through an authorization drawn from the Highway Trust Fund. To the extent consensus rulemaking lets railroads slow or water down safety standards the FRA might otherwise issue on its own, the cost would fall on people living and working near rail lines and on rail workers themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; potentially communities near rail lines

drawbacks.text: The committee operates by consensus among stakeholders, which means the freight railroads being regulated hold a formal veto over recommendations for their own safety rules; consensus bodies like this are widely understood to move slowly and to favor the least-agreeable participant.
The bill directs no new safety standard of its own—no requirement on braking, staffing, or hazardous materials—so its only substantive effect is procedural.

It authorizes spending from the Highway Trust Fund, a fund already stretched by road and transit needs, to pay for a committee whose funding mechanism the FRA previously handled as an ordinary agency expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real benefit is permanence and accountability for a process that exists today, plus guaranteed seats for rail labor and passenger advocates. Its real cost is institutional: it hardens a consensus system in which the regulated industry sits as co-author of its own safety rules, which tends to produce slower and weaker standards than direct agency rulemaking. The bill contains no safety requirement for railroads to comply with, so a reader should judge it as a change in who writes the rules, not as a safety improvement in itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2026, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Railroads subcommittee, and has stayed there with no cosponsors and no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes (D-OH) introduced the bill on February 3, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, and the sponsor gave introductory remarks on the House floor.
No member has signed on as a cosponsor.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has been recorded since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained—the status quo holds. The freight railroads keep the existing, informal version of the consensus process they already participate in, and the FRA keeps full discretion over how and whether to use it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo, favoring railroads and FRA discretion

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory floor remarks, and became its only supporter in the chamber.

sides.party_line_note: No opposition is recorded anywhere in the record, but neither is any support beyond the sponsor: with zero cosponsors [S3] and no committee or floor action, the bill has simply not drawn enough interest to move.

industries.note: Codifying the committee permanently locks in the industry's seat in negotiated rulemaking, where consensus among members gives each stakeholder block, including the railroads being regulated, leverage over the safety standards that govern them. The industry's interest in a consensus process runs against the public's interest in prompt, stringent safety rules, though it also produces rules both sides can accept.

The bill guarantees seats for organizations representing every rail craft, giving workers a permanent, formal role in safety rulemaking. Their leverage under consensus rules runs alongside worker and public safety, though consensus also tempers union demands when the industry digs in.

Equipment suppliers and manufacturers get a guaranteed seat in crafting the safety standards for the products they sell. Their interest in workable, affordable standards partly aligns with the public's and partly with the railroads' preference for lower compliance costs.

industries.industry: Passenger rail (Amtrak and passenger advocacy organizations)
industries.note: Amtrak and rail passenger organizations each receive at least one guaranteed seat, formalizing their voice in safety rules that affect the trains their passengers ride.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors [S3], no subcommittee action in the months since referral [S4], and no companion legislation, the bill follows the path of most single-sponsor transportation bills in the second session of a Congress: it will likely sit in the Railroads subcommittee and expire at the end of the session unless its sponsor attracts support or attaches it to a larger rail or surface transportation package.
